client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup about a month ago. The hours are just brutal — I'm staying late almost every night, and by the time I get home I'm completely drained but somehow still can't sleep because my mind keeps racing about everything I didn't finish. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the workload is just... real, you know? It's not like therapy can make my boss assign me fewer tasks.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a real, heavy load right now — the exhaustion, the sleeplessness, the sense that your mind won't let you rest even when your body desperately needs it. You're absolutely right that I can't reduce your workload, and I want to honor that this situation is genuinely demanding, not just a matter of perception. What I *can* help with is how your thoughts about the unfinished work might be amplifying the stress beyond the work itself — so I'm curious, when your mind is racing at night, what kinds of thoughts tend to show up most?

client: Honestly, the thoughts that keep coming up are things like "if I don't finish this by tomorrow, everything will fall apart" or "I'm already behind and it's only going to get worse." There's this constant loop of going through everything I haven't done yet, almost like my brain is making a list over and over just to torture me. And underneath all of that, there's this feeling that I'm somehow failing, like I should be able to handle this better than I am.
therapist: That loop your brain is running sounds genuinely exhausting — like a mental alarm that keeps going off even when there's nothing more you can do at midnight. I want to gently point to something: that thought "I *should* be able to handle this better" is doing a lot of quiet damage, because it adds a layer of self-judgment on top of an already hard situation. When you imagine someone you care about starting a demanding new job and struggling with the hours — would you tell *them* they should be handling it better, or would you see their struggle as a pretty understandable response to a tough circumstance?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them it makes total sense that they're struggling. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to be tougher than that, or I've had enough time to adjust by now and I'm just not.
therapist: There's something really important in what you just noticed — you'd offer a friend genuine compassion, but you're holding yourself to a completely different, harsher standard. That belief that you should be "tougher" or adjusted by now is worth examining, because one month into a brutal startup schedule isn't really enough time to adapt — that's not a personal failing, that's just reality. Where do you think that expectation of toughness comes from — is it something this job brought out, or does it feel more familiar than that?

client: Honestly, it feels really familiar — like it's been there my whole life, not just this job. I grew up in a house where showing struggle was kind of seen as weakness, so you just pushed through and didn't make a big deal out of things. I guess I internalized that pretty deeply, because even now I feel almost embarrassed admitting that the schedule is getting to me.
therapist: What you're sharing takes real courage, and the fact that you feel embarrassed admitting struggle is itself a sign of how deeply that early message got woven into who you are — it wasn't a choice you made, it was something you absorbed to survive your environment. That little kid who learned to push through was being smart and adaptive, but that same rule is now costing you a lot as an adult, because it's blocking you from giving yourself the care you'd so readily offer someone else. I'm wondering — when you imagine slowly loosening that old rule, even just a little, what feels scary about letting yourself acknowledge that this is genuinely hard?

client: I think what scares me is that if I actually admit it's hard, I won't be able to stop... like I'll just fall apart completely and never pull myself back together. There's this fear that acknowledging the struggle makes it more real, more permanent somehow, like I'm giving it permission to take over. And honestly, part of me worries that if I let myself feel it, I'll just become someone who's constantly overwhelmed and needy, and then I'll really end up alone.
therapist: That fear — that feeling it fully means being consumed by it forever — is one of the most common and painful traps our minds set for us, and it makes so much sense given where you learned to cope. But I want to offer a gentle challenge to that belief: in your experience, when you've allowed yourself to briefly acknowledge something hard, did you actually fall apart and stay there, or did the feeling move through and eventually shift? And that fear of becoming "needy" and ending up alone — that tells me there's a really deep loneliness already underneath all this pushing through, and I wonder if the armor that was meant to protect you from that might actually be keeping connection at a distance.

client: I hate that what you're saying actually makes sense, because part of me really wants to push back on it. When I think about the times I've let something slip through... yeah, I didn't completely fall apart, but it still felt awful and I spent days worrying I'd said too much or shown too much to someone. And the loneliness thing — you're right that it's already there, I feel it constantly, but somehow the idea of letting people see that and then still ending up alone feels so much worse than just staying numb and lonely on my own terms.
therapist: There's something really profound in what you just said — that staying numb and lonely "on your own terms" feels safer than risking being seen and still ending up alone, because at least then you're in control of the pain. That's not weakness, that's actually a very logical strategy your mind developed to protect you from what might feel like the worst possible outcome. But I want to sit with this gently — when you imagine someone truly seeing your struggle and *not* leaving, even if that feels hard to believe right now, what comes up for you?

client: I mean... when I try to imagine that, there's this weird mix of things that comes up. Part of me feels something almost like relief, like a tiny flicker of it, but then it gets immediately drowned out by this voice that says "that's not real, that doesn't actually happen for people like you." It's like I can't even let myself stay in that image for more than a second before my brain starts poking holes in it.
therapist: That tiny flicker of relief is actually really significant — it means some part of you *does* want to be seen and held, even if it gets quickly shouted down. I want to gently name that voice — "that doesn't happen for people like me" — because that's not a fact your brain discovered, it's a conclusion a younger version of you drew from painful experiences, and it's been running quietly in the background ever since. What do you think "people like you" means in that moment — what is your brain actually saying you are?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. When I try to actually look at what my brain is saying... it's something like "too much, too needy, the kind of person who drives people away if they get too close." I've never really put words to it like that before and it feels uncomfortably accurate, which is kind of unsettling.
therapist: The fact that putting words to it feels unsettling is actually a sign that something real and important just surfaced — you've been carrying that belief quietly for so long that naming it out loud makes it suddenly visible in a new way. I want to be careful here, because "too much, too needy, drives people away" — that's not a truth about who you are, it's a story that was likely written for you by early experiences where your needs *weren't* met, and your young mind made it mean something was wrong with *you* rather than with the situation. I'm curious — can you think of even one relationship in your life, past or present, where someone got close to you and *didn't* leave or pull away?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, everyone eventually pulls back. But there's my friend Dara, she's been around for like six years and she hasn't gone anywhere, even when I've been a mess. I don't know though, sometimes I wonder if she just hasn't gotten tired of me yet, like maybe I'm on borrowed time with her too.
therapist: Dara is really important evidence here — six years, seen you at your worst, still there, and your brain's response is to reframe that as borrowed time rather than let it count. That's how deep this belief runs: it doesn't just ignore contradictions, it *explains them away* to protect itself from being wrong. I wonder what it would mean for you — about yourself, about your life — if you allowed Dara's six years of showing up to actually be real and count as proof?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but when I actually try to let it count, like really sit with it, there's this almost physical resistance, like my chest tightens up. If Dara's six years are real proof, then that means I've been wrong about myself this whole time, and I don't know if that's comforting or just... terrifying. It's like, who even am I if the story I've been telling myself about being fundamentally alone and unlovable isn't true?
therapist: What you're sitting with right now is one of the most disorienting and courageous moments a person can have — because our stories about ourselves, even the painful ones, become a kind of home, and questioning them can feel like the ground shifting beneath you. That tightness in your chest is real, and it makes complete sense, because you're not just updating a small belief — you're touching something that has organized your whole way of moving through the world and protecting yourself. And I want to offer this gently: the question "who am I if I'm not fundamentally unlovable" isn't a crisis — it's actually the most important and alive question you've ever let yourself ask.
